texts.0: SP, due to a late power reduction and failure to re-trim after establishing the descent, did not stabilize the penetration airspeed on the value published for the procedure. Airspeed accelerated to about 20 knots above the target and stayed there through the descent, well beyond the +15 knot limit. IP intervened with power and speed brake to recover the parameter before the final approach segment.
texts.1: SP, due to an incorrect power-to-attitude relationship set at descent entry, allowed the penetration airspeed to reach 15 knots above the target, at the outer limit of the tolerance. The deviation was reduced only after the IP called the airspeed twice, and the correction was applied slowly. No IP control input was required, but the parameter was re-established late in the descent.
texts.2: SP, due to a nose-low attitude carried after the descent entry, let the penetration airspeed increase to about 12 knots above the target, outside the +10 knot standard. SP recognized the trend on the next cross-check, reduced power promptly and brought the airspeed back inside tolerance without any prompt from the IP. The remainder of the descent was flown on speed.
texts.3: SP set power and attitude accurately at descent entry and held the penetration airspeed within +10/-5 knots throughout the procedure. Corrections were small, early and made with the power lever rather than with attitude excursions. The aircraft was on speed at the transition to the final approach segment.
texts.4: SP established the penetration airspeed at descent entry and held it essentially on the published value for the whole descent, with deviations of only a few knots. Power and trim were used with anticipation, so no corrective action of any size became necessary. The aircraft arrived at the final approach segment exactly on speed.
texts.marginal: SP kept the penetration airspeed within standards but consistently on the fast side, close to the +10 knot boundary, and each correction was made after the deviation rather than in anticipation of it. The trend was for the speed to increase whenever attention shifted to the navigation tasks. SP is expected to anticipate the power requirement at descent entry and to hold the target speed within a narrower working band.

texts_at.0: SP flew the penetration with the IP setting power at descent entry and talking through the airspeed indicator scan through the descent. This is SP's first exposure to penetration airspeed control, and re-trimming after establishing the descent has not yet become a habit. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to begin re-trimming independently after establishing the descent, with the IP available to call any trend that develops.
texts_at.1: SP stabilized penetration airspeed to the standard expected at this stage, letting it reach 15 knots above target, at the outer limit of the tolerance, before it was reduced. The reduction followed the IP calling the airspeed twice rather than SP's own early cross-check. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to bring the airspeed indicator into the scan at descent entry rather than only after the IP has called it.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the trend on the next cross-check without any prompt from the IP, letting airspeed increase to about 12 knots above target, outside the +10 knot standard, before reducing power promptly. The nose-low attitude carried after descent entry is still allowed to build the trend before it is corrected. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to check pitch against power at descent entry so the trend does not need a separate correction.
texts_at.3: SP set power and attitude accurately at descent entry and held the penetration airspeed within +10/-5 knots throughout the procedure on most of the descent, with corrections small, early and made with the power lever. One correction was slightly later than the rest, without leaving the standard. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to make that correction as promptly as the rest of the descent.

texts_above.1: SP stabilized penetration airspeed, letting it reach about 15 knots above target, at the tolerance limit, before it was reduced. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the trend on the next cross-check without any prompt from the IP, letting airspeed increase to about 12 knots above target before reducing power promptly. Checking pitch against power at descent entry, rather than letting the trend build first, would keep that increase smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good power-and-attitude coordination.
texts_above.3: SP set power and attitude accurately at descent entry and held the penetration airspeed within +10/-5 knots throughout the procedure, with corrections small, early and made with the power lever rather than with attitude excursions, arriving on speed at the transition to final approach. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good speed discipline.
texts_above.4: SP established the penetration airspeed at descent entry and held it essentially on the published value for the whole descent, with power and trim used with anticipation so no corrective action of any size became necessary. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent airspeed anticipation.

texts.0: SP, due to an uncorrected drift and no wind allowance applied on the inbound radial, did not maintain the published course during the penetration. Course displacement reached about 12 degrees and continued to increase, well beyond the +/- 8 degree limit. IP took control of heading to regain the radial before the aircraft left the protected area of the procedure.
texts.1: SP, due to chasing the course needle with large heading changes instead of holding a computed correction, allowed the displacement from the penetration radial to reach 8 degrees, at the limit of tolerance. SP re-centred the needle only after the IP pointed out the displacement, and the correction overshot before settling. The aircraft stayed inside the procedure, but the course was regained late in the descent.
texts.2: SP, due to a late recognition of the crosswind component in the descending turn, drifted about 7 degrees off the penetration radial, outside the +/- 5 degree standard. SP identified the displacement on the following cross-check, applied a suitable wind correction angle and re-established the radial without any prompt from the IP. Course was then held for the rest of the descent.
texts.3: SP tracked the penetration radial within +/- 5 degrees throughout the descent, applying a wind correction angle from the start of the procedure. Heading corrections were small and made before the needle displacement could grow. The aircraft was established on course at the start of the final approach segment.
texts.4: SP flew the penetration radial with the needle essentially centred for the entire descent, using a wind correction angle that was set early and refined by small amounts. No displacement large enough to require a correction developed at any point. The aircraft reached the final approach segment precisely on course.
texts.marginal: SP remained within the course tolerance, but the needle was allowed to displace to about 4 to 5 degrees before each correction, and the corrections were made in steps rather than continuously. The pattern showed a repeated drift to the same side of the radial that was reacted to instead of being anticipated. SP is expected to establish an accurate wind correction angle early and to keep the working band well inside the standard.

texts_at.0: SP tracked the penetration radial with the IP setting the wind correction angle and talking through recognizing the crosswind in the descending turn. This is SP's first exposure to tracking course during a descent, and holding a computed correction rather than chasing the needle has not yet been built. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to begin holding a computed correction independently rather than chasing the needle, with the IP available to confirm the angle.
texts_at.1: SP tracked the penetration radial to the standard expected at this stage, letting displacement reach 8 degrees, at the limit of tolerance, before it was re-centred. The re-centring followed the IP pointing out the displacement rather than SP's own recognition of the crosswind. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to recognize the crosswind component in the descending turn rather than needing the displacement pointed out.
texts_at.2: SP identified the displacement on the following cross-check without any prompt from the IP, letting drift reach about 7 degrees off the penetration radial, outside the +/- 5 degree standard, before applying a suitable wind correction angle. The crosswind component in the descending turn is still recognized late rather than at roll-in. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to assess the crosswind as the descending turn is rolled into rather than after it is established.
texts_at.3: SP tracked the penetration radial within +/- 5 degrees throughout the descent on most of it, applying a wind correction angle from the start of the procedure with heading corrections small and made before the needle displacement could grow. One correction needed a slightly larger adjustment following a wind shift, without leaving the standard. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to make that adjustment as promptly as the rest of the descent.

texts_above.1: SP tracked the penetration radial, letting displacement reach about 8 degrees, at the tolerance limit, before it was re-centred. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP identified the displacement on the following cross-check without any prompt from the IP, letting drift reach about 7 degrees off the penetration radial before applying a suitable wind correction angle. Assessing the crosswind as the descending turn is rolled into, rather than after it is established, would keep that drift smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound wind-correction technique.
texts_above.3: SP tracked the penetration radial within +/- 5 degrees throughout the descent, applying a wind correction angle from the start of the procedure with heading corrections small and made before the needle displacement could grow, established on course at the start of the final approach segment. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed course tracking.
texts_above.4: SP flew the penetration radial with the needle essentially centred for the entire descent, using a wind correction angle set early and refined by small amounts, reaching the final approach segment precisely on course. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional drift-correction accuracy.

texts.0: SP, due to an unstandard read-back that did not confirm the actual clearance, began the penetration on a descent clearance that had not been issued. The ATC instruction was misapplied and the aircraft entered the procedure without approval to descend, departing the assigned altitude by more than 300 ft before IP intervened, stopped the descent and coordinated the correct clearance with the controller.
texts.1: SP, due to a read-back that did not confirm the assigned altitude, did not comply with the ATC instruction as issued and set the wrong level for the descent, off by 300 ft at the tolerance limit. SP corrected the setting only after the IP repeated the clearance on interphone, and the confirming transmission to ATC was delayed. No IP control input was necessary.
texts.2: SP, due to a transmission made while the descent checks were still in progress, acknowledged the ATC descent instruction incompletely and initially set an intermediate altitude, about 200 ft off the assigned level, between the tolerances. SP re-checked the clearance, corrected the setting and confirmed with the controller without prompting, well before the aircraft approached the wrong level. All subsequent instructions were complied with as issued.
texts.3: SP complied with every ATC instruction during the penetration, read back the clearances in standard phraseology and set the assigned altitudes correctly. Requests and reports were made in good time and did not interfere with the flying of the procedure. No clarification from the controller or the IP was required.
texts.4: SP complied with every ATC instruction promptly and precisely, with concise standard read-backs that confirmed each element of the clearance. Radio work was integrated into the descent with no effect on aircraft control. Coordination with the controller was complete before it was needed at each point of the procedure.
texts.marginal: SP complied with all ATC instructions, but the read-backs were slow and on two occasions a second transmission was needed to confirm the assigned altitude. The trend was for radio work to accumulate at the busiest points of the descent instead of being cleared early. SP is expected to use concise standard phraseology and to complete each transmission before entering the next segment of the penetration.

texts_at.0: SP worked the ATC clearance with the IP confirming the assigned altitude in the read-back and talking through standard phraseology for the descent. This is SP's first exposure to reading back a descent clearance under workload, and confirming the assigned altitude in the read-back itself has not yet become routine. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to begin confirming the assigned altitude independently in the read-back, with the IP available to confirm the clearance.
texts_at.1: SP handled the ATC clearance to the standard expected at this stage, setting the wrong level for the descent by 300 ft, at the tolerance limit, before it was corrected. texts_at.2: SP re-checked the clearance and corrected the setting without prompting, letting the intermediate altitude sit about 200 ft off the assigned level, between the tolerances, before it was confirmed with the controller. The transmission is still made while the descent checks are in progress rather than after them. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. texts_at.3: SP complied with every ATC instruction during the penetration, read back the clearances in standard phraseology and set the assigned altitudes correctly on most of the descent, with requests and reports made in good time. Completing the descent checks before transmitting, rather than mid-task, would keep that error from appearing at all. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid clearance handling.

Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate readback discipline.
texts_above.4: SP complied with every ATC instruction promptly and precisely, with concise standard read-backs that confirmed each element of the clearance, integrating radio work into the descent with no effect on aircraft control. texts.0: SP, due to lack of awareness of a published restriction that was available in the briefing material, did not observe the altitude restriction of the penetration as depicted in the Instrument Approach Manual. The aircraft descended more than 300 ft below the published segment minimum before reaching the fix. IP intervened to arrest the descent and re-establish the aircraft on the published profile.
texts.1: SP, due to an incomplete review of the routing published for the procedure, applied the step-down restriction late and continued down to within 300 ft of the segment minimum before the fix, at the tolerance limit. The profile was corrected only after the IP called the restriction, and the level-off was flown at the limiting altitude with no margin. No IP control input was required.
texts.2: SP, due to a rate of descent that was not adjusted for the distance remaining, arrived early at the published step-down altitude and began to close on the restriction, coming within about 200 ft of it, between the tolerances. SP recognized the developing profile error on the DME cross-check, reduced the rate of descent and met the restriction with margin, without prompting. All remaining restrictions of the procedure were observed.
texts.3: SP observed every routing and altitude restriction published in MAIP and the Instrument Approach Manual throughout the penetration. Step-down altitudes were identified in advance and the descent profile was flown against DME so that each restriction was met with margin. No restriction was approached without a deliberate check.
texts.4: SP flew the published routing exactly and met every altitude restriction of the procedure with a planned and comfortable margin. Each fix and step-down was identified and called before it was reached, so the profile never required a rate change to remain within the published limits. The aircraft was in the published position and altitude at every point of the descent.
texts.marginal: SP did not violate any routing or altitude restriction, but the descent was flown close to the published minima and the step-downs were identified only as they were reached. The trend was a reactive rather than a planned use of the DME and altitude information. SP is expected to build the descent profile before entry and to keep a deliberate margin above each published restriction.

texts_at.0: SP flew the routing with the IP calling each altitude restriction and talking through building the descent profile against DME before entry. This is SP's first exposure to a published step-down profile, and building the descent profile before entry has not yet been built. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to begin building the descent profile independently before entry, with the IP available to confirm each restriction.
texts_at.1: SP observed the altitude restriction to the standard expected at this stage, continuing down to within 300 ft of the segment minimum, at the tolerance limit, before the level-off. The level-off followed the IP calling the restriction rather than SP's own review of the routing. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to review the published routing before the descent begins rather than applying restrictions late as they are reached.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the developing profile error on the DME cross-check without prompting, coming within about 200 ft of the restriction, between the tolerances, before reducing the rate of descent to meet it with margin. The rate of descent is still not adjusted for the remaining distance before the error develops. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to adjust the rate of descent for the remaining distance from the outset rather than correcting it once a margin has already closed.
texts_at.3: SP observed every routing and altitude restriction published in MAIP and the Instrument Approach Manual throughout the penetration on most of it, with step-down altitudes identified in advance and the descent profile flown against DME so each restriction was met with margin. One restriction was met with a slightly narrower margin, without being violated. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to keep that margin as comfortable as the rest of the procedure.

texts_above.1: SP observed the altitude restriction, continuing down to within about 300 ft of the segment minimum, at the tolerance limit, before the level-off. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the developing profile error on the DME cross-check without prompting, coming within about 200 ft of the restriction before reducing the rate of descent to meet it with margin. Adjusting the rate of descent for the remaining distance from the outset, rather than once a margin has closed, would keep that margin wider from the start. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady profile management.

texts.0: SP, due to omission of the descent checks before the procedure, did not execute the penetration according to the standardized sequence described in the Techniques and Procedures Manual. The navigation aid was not tuned and identified and the aircraft entered the descent in the wrong configuration, with the course drifting more than 8 degrees off the penetration radial while the items were sorted out. IP intervened to complete the items and re-order the procedure.
texts.1: SP, due to an out-of-order execution of the descent checks, did not follow the standardized sequence for the penetration and left the navigation aid identification until after the descent had begun. The outstanding items were completed only after the IP called them, and the course drifted to 8 degrees off the radial, at the tolerance limit, while the procedure was flown one step behind for the rest of the descent. No IP control input was required.
texts.2: SP, due to starting the descent checks late, executed two items of the penetration sequence out of the order described in the Techniques and Procedures Manual, with the course drifting about 6 degrees off the radial while the discrepancy was being resolved. SP recognized the discrepancy before the descent point, completed the outstanding items and restored the standard sequence without prompting. The remainder of the procedure was flown in order and without mistakes.
texts.3: SP executed the penetration according to the standardized procedure, with descent checks, navigation aid tuning and identification and configuration changes completed in the published order and at the correct points. No item was omitted and no correction by the IP was needed. The procedure was flown as described in the Techniques and Procedures Manual and AFMAN 11-202 Vol 3.
texts.4: SP executed the whole penetration in the standard sequence, with every item completed ahead of the point at which it was required. Checks, navigation aid selection and configuration changes were positioned so that no task overlapped a critical part of the descent. The procedure was flown without a single departure from the published technique.
texts.marginal: SP executed the penetration in the correct sequence and without mistakes, but several items were completed at the last moment before the point at which they were required. The trend was for the checks to compress into the descent entry instead of being finished before it. SP is expected to bring the sequence forward so that each item is complete with margin ahead of its trigger point.

error_modes.label: LEVEL-OFF AND TRANSITION TO FINAL APPROACH

texts.0: SP, due to no lead point computed for the level-off, did not arrest the descent at the assigned altitude and continued through it during the transition to final approach. The aircraft continued more than 300 ft below the assigned altitude while the airspeed decayed more than 10 knots below target during the recovery attempt. IP intervened to level the aircraft and establish it for the final approach segment.
texts.1: SP, due to a rate of descent that was not reduced approaching the assigned altitude, levelled off late and applied power only after the speed had fallen 10 knots below target, at the limit of the tolerance. The level-off was completed after the IP called the altitude, and the aircraft entered the final approach segment slow and still being corrected. No IP control input was required.
texts.2: SP, due to a late power addition at the level-off, allowed the airspeed to fall about 8 knots below the target as the aircraft was established for the final approach, outside the -5 knot standard. SP recognized the decay immediately, added power and regained the target speed before the final approach segment began. The transition was then completed on altitude and on course.
texts.3: SP planned the level-off with an appropriate lead, arrested the descent at the assigned altitude and transitioned to the final approach segment on speed and on course. Power was added in time, so no airspeed excursion developed. The aircraft was stable and correctly configured when the final approach began.
texts.4: SP levelled off at the assigned altitude with an anticipated lead and no perceptible overshoot, and delivered the aircraft to the final approach segment exactly on altitude, speed and course. Power was set before the speed could change, so the transition required no correction at all. The aircraft was fully stable at the start of the final approach.
texts.marginal: SP completed the level-off and the transition to final approach within standards, but the lead was taken late and the aircraft settled onto the assigned altitude after a small overshoot on each occasion. The trend was to correct the profile at the last moment instead of planning the lead from the rate of descent. SP is expected to compute the level-off lead and to arrive at the final approach segment stable and without corrections.

texts_at.0: SP flew the level-off with the IP calling the rate of descent approaching the assigned altitude and talking through adding power as the level-off begins. This is SP's first exposure to planning a level-off lead, and reducing the rate of descent approaching the assigned altitude has not yet been built. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to begin reducing the rate of descent independently approaching the assigned altitude, with the IP available to confirm the lead.
texts_at.1: SP planned the level-off to the standard expected at this stage, letting the speed fall 10 knots below target, at the limit of the tolerance, before power was applied. The level-off followed the IP calling the altitude rather than SP's own reduced rate of descent. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to reduce the rate of descent approaching the assigned altitude rather than continuing it to the level-off point.

IP took control of the heading to regain the radial before the aircraft left the protected area of the procedure.

The lead point is still computed without allowing for the descending turn on that occasion. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to compute the lead point for the descending turn on every turn, not only most of them.
texts_at.3: SP used lead points for the turns during the penetration, so each roll-out was on the published course within plus or minus 5 degrees, on most turns, made with constant bank and without corrections after roll-out. One turn needed a small intercept following a slightly optimistic lead, without leaving the standard. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to compute that turn's lead as accurately as the rest.

texts_above.1: SP used a lead point for turns during the penetration, letting displacement reach about 8 degrees, at the tolerance limit, before the intercept back to the radial was started. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the displacement on the following cross-check without prompting, letting the roll-out land about 7 degrees off the penetration radial before taking an intercept heading and re-establishing the course. Computing the lead point for the descending turn on every turn, not only most of them, would remove that displacement. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent lead-point computation.
texts_above.3: SP used lead points for the turns during the penetration, so each roll-out was on the published course within plus or minus 5 degrees, made with constant bank and without corrections after the roll-out, preserving the smoothness of the descent. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to disciplined turn planning.
texts_above.4: SP computed a lead point for every turn from the groundspeed and the angle to be turned, and each roll-out placed the aircraft on the course with the needle essentially centred, with no intercept needed at any point of the procedure. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to faultless lead-point accuracy.

error_modes.label: AIRFIELD REVIEW BEFORE THE IFR ARRIVAL

texts.0: SP, due to relying on prior familiarity with the destination instead of reviewing the airfield information before the arrival, entered the descent without current knowledge of the field elevation, runway data and glide path guidance available. The wrong minimum altitude was set for the procedure and the aircraft was descended more than 300 ft below the published profile of the arrival. IP intervened to stop the descent and to establish the aircraft on the correct arrival routing and altitude.
texts.1: SP, due to a review of the airfield information that was left until the descent had begun, was not familiar with the approach lighting and the tower frequency in use, and the arrival was flown with the wrong frequency selected, with the aircraft settling about 300 ft off the published profile, at the tolerance limit. The correct data were obtained only after the IP directed the review, and the delay caused the aircraft to be established on the course late. No IP control input was necessary.
texts.2: SP, due to reviewing only part of the airfield data before the arrival, had to look up the field elevation and runway data during the penetration. The attention given to that task allowed the course to drift about 7 degrees off the radial, outside the plus or minus 5 degree standard, before SP re-established the tracking without prompting and completed the review at a quieter point.
texts.3: SP reviewed the airfield layout, approach lighting, glide path guidance, field elevation, runway data and the tower and ground frequencies before the arrival, even though the field had been visited before. Nothing had to be looked up during the descent and the procedure was flown within all tolerances. The arrival was set up before the top-of-descent point.
texts.4: SP completed a full review of the airfield information before the arrival and confirmed the significant items again on the way down, so every setting was already made when it was needed. The descent required no reference to publications and the aircraft was flown within a few degrees of the course throughout. Prior familiarity was treated as preparation rather than as a substitute for the review.
texts.marginal: SP reviewed the airfield information and flew the arrival within standards, but the review was brief and based mainly on previous knowledge of the field, so two items had to be confirmed during the descent. The trend was for that confirmation to compete with the flying of the procedure and to let the course drift towards the tolerance boundary. SP is expected to complete the airfield review before the arrival regardless of previous familiarity with the field.

texts_at.0: SP reviewed the airfield information with the IP talking through the layout, the lighting, the glide path guidance and the runway data before the arrival. This is SP's first exposure to a full pre-arrival airfield review, and completing it before the descent begins has not yet become a fixed habit. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to begin completing the airfield review independently before the descent, with the IP available to confirm the items.
texts_at.1: SP reviewed the airfield information to the standard expected at this stage, with the aircraft settling about 300 ft off the published profile, at the tolerance limit, before the correct data were obtained. The correction followed the IP directing the review rather than SP's own preparation. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to complete the airfield review before the descent begins, not after it has already started.
texts_at.2: SP re-established the tracking without prompting, letting the course drift about 7 degrees off the radial, outside the plus or minus 5 degree standard, while the field elevation and runway data were looked up during the penetration. The review is still completed only in part before the arrival rather than in full. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to complete the whole review before the arrival so nothing has to be looked up during the descent.
texts_at.3: SP reviewed the airfield layout, approach lighting, glide path guidance, field elevation, runway data and the tower and ground frequencies before the arrival on most items, with nothing looked up during the descent and the procedure flown within all tolerances. One item was confirmed a little later than the rest, without affecting the descent. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to review that item as early as the rest of the briefing.

texts_above.1: SP reviewed the airfield information, with the aircraft settling about 300 ft off the published profile, at the tolerance limit, before the correct data were obtained. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP re-established the tracking without prompting, letting the course drift about 7 degrees off the radial while the field elevation and runway data were looked up during the penetration. Completing the whole review before the arrival, rather than only in part, would remove that drift. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good airfield-review discipline.
texts_above.3: SP reviewed the airfield layout, approach lighting, glide path guidance, field elevation, runway data and the tower and ground frequencies before the arrival, even though the field had been visited before, with nothing looked up during the descent and the arrival set up before the top-of-descent point. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good arrival preparation.
texts_above.4: SP completed a full review of the airfield information before the arrival and confirmed the significant items again on the way down, so every setting was already made when it was needed, with prior familiarity treated as preparation rather than as a substitute for the review. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent arrival readiness.

error_modes.label: ARRIVAL AND APPROACH SELECTION AT THE DESTINATION

texts.0: SP, due to selecting an arrival procedure that required extensive cruise at low altitude before the descent, planned an arrival that did not match the training objectives of the sortie and consumed fuel at an excessive rate. The aircraft was held low and slow far from the field, the plan was then changed while the descent was in progress and the published routing was no longer being followed, with the course drifting more than 8 degrees off the assigned radial during the replan. IP intervened to re-plan the arrival with the controller and to re-establish the aircraft on the procedure.
texts.1: SP, due to choosing an arrival that placed the aircraft at low altitude earlier than necessary, created a fuel situation that required a change of plan during the descent. The revised routing was requested only after the IP raised the fuel state, and the coordination with approach control was made late, with the course drifting to 8 degrees off the radial, at the tolerance limit, before the routing was re-confirmed. No IP control input was required and the aircraft remained on the assigned routing.
texts.2: SP, due to a request for an additional approach that was not coordinated with approach control early enough, received a re-routing at a busy point of the descent. Reorganizing the procedure took attention from the navigation and the course was allowed to drift about 7 degrees off the radial, outside the plus or minus 5 degree standard, before SP re-established it without any prompt from the IP.
texts.3: SP selected an arrival and approach that matched the training objectives of the sortie and did not require extensive cruise at low altitude. Requests for additional approaches were coordinated with approach control early and SP remained flexible when an alternative was offered. The descent was flown within all tolerances and with a comfortable fuel state.
texts.4: SP planned the arrival around the training objectives and the fuel available, coordinated every request with approach control well in advance and accepted alternatives without any disturbance to the procedure. The aircraft was never held at low altitude longer than the routing required. The descent was flown precisely and the fuel state remained well ahead of the plan.
texts.marginal: SP selected a workable arrival and stayed within standards, but the choice left the aircraft at low altitude longer than necessary and the request for the additional approach was made only as the descent began. The trend was to coordinate at the point of need rather than as early as possible, which compressed the descent planning. SP is expected to match the arrival to the training objectives and to coordinate requests with approach control well before they are required.

texts_at.0: SP selected the arrival with the IP talking through matching the routing to the training objectives and coordinating requests with approach control early. This is SP's first exposure to selecting an arrival that matches the training objectives, and coordinating requests with approach control early has not yet become routine. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to begin coordinating requests with approach control independently and early, with the IP available to confirm the plan.
texts_at.1: SP selected an arrival to the standard expected at this stage, with the course drifting to 8 degrees off the radial, at the tolerance limit, before the routing was re-confirmed. The re-confirmation followed the IP raising the fuel state rather than SP's own early planning. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to choose an arrival that does not place the aircraft at low altitude earlier than necessary, so a fuel-driven change of plan is not needed.
texts_at.2: SP re-established the course without any prompt from the IP, letting it drift about 7 degrees off the radial, outside the plus or minus 5 degree standard, while the re-routing from an uncoordinated request was being absorbed. The request for the additional approach is still made later than it could be, close to the point of need. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to coordinate the request for an additional approach earlier so the re-routing does not arrive at a busy point of the descent.
texts_at.3: SP selected an arrival and approach that matched the training objectives of the sortie and did not require extensive cruise at low altitude on most of the sortie, with requests for additional approaches coordinated with approach control early and flown within all tolerances. One coordination came a little later than planned, without affecting the profile. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to coordinate that request as early as the rest of the sortie.

texts_above.1: SP selected an arrival, with the course drifting to about 8 degrees off the radial, at the tolerance limit, before the routing was re-confirmed. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP re-established the course without any prompt from the IP, letting it drift about 7 degrees off the radial while the re-routing from an uncoordinated request was being absorbed. Coordinating the request for an additional approach earlier, rather than close to the point of need, would keep the re-routing from landing at a busy point of the descent. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady arrival planning.
texts_above.3: SP selected an arrival and approach that matched the training objectives of the sortie and did not require extensive cruise at low altitude, coordinating requests for additional approaches with approach control early and remaining flexible when an alternative was offered, flown within all tolerances and with a comfortable fuel state. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good fuel-and-routing planning.
texts_above.4: SP planned the arrival around the training objectives and the fuel available, coordinated every request with approach control well in advance and accepted alternatives without disturbance to the procedure, never held at low altitude longer than the routing required. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior arrival management.
